# **Judgement Hour(s)**

There are a lot of thoughts I have about the fair and how I felt.

I think the beginning set the tone of the fair. I was really nervous at the beginning and somewhat hesitant to present my project to people. But, Pyotr coming up to my booth and being my test participant along with Dr. Lu coming up to me to check out my project (even if it was for grading) really helped boost my mood and energize me for the next 40 minutes. I really appreciated their help.

I wanted to show demo footage on my second monitor, but I never had time to record so I instead put up a video of the video that inspired me to learn about glitching: Takeshi Murata’s *Monster Movie*. Then, I realized how hard it was trying to tell people how to launch the game when I couldn’t see what they were doing, so I wired the VR headset to my laptop and launched it myself. Fortunately, that fixed the whole see what the game was issue.

I was really happy to see my HDCC106 professor Dr. Bollmer. We had a nice conversation about the hostile nature of glitching and how contradictory it feels compared to standard VR practices (i.e. try not to make the player throw up).

There was a guy that came up to me and said that he spent his childhood writing data onto floppy disks. I unfortunately couldn’t really connect with him when talking, and I felt bad because my depictions of editing data weren’t necessarily accurate to the real world. 

I enjoyed watching people play my game and live commentating what they were seeing, but it felt like a lot of people struggled to get through the hoop that was being comfortable in Virtual Reality. A lot of people weren’t familiar with the buttons they could press and movement was a dance between using the joysticks and physically turning and reaching. Many participants were just enamored with the spectacle of virtual reality that further engaging with my game (such as experimentation with messing with the file data) was rare. 

Overall, I felt an unnatural energy in me throughout the fair and I think that I did a decent job presenting.

# **Post Mortem**

## **The Semester**

The work spread in this semester was extremely unbalanced. I do not believe that I put enough effort until I had a month left, partly because I feel I did not take the capstone as seriously as I should have. I feel like I ended up abusing the design phase of my project to slack off under the pretense of brainstorming. While I did well in finalizing the core mechanics of the game and visualizing the end product, I also felt I stayed too long in the design period. Additionally, I began to fall behind in the HDCC209 assignments.   
The final product, at least in my eyes, felt like the result of a one-month sprint rather than a 3-month jog (ok well not a one-month sprint more like a 2-month leisurely walk and then a month sprint).

Despite this, I felt like I did good work. I am really happy with the phonograph model that I made for the audio device and I had a lot of fun modeling in blender and creating visual effects in Unity. I feel I have learned a lot in terms of technical skills and this project let me hit the ground running with Blender and the 3D design pipeline.

## **The Fair**

Due to my progress, the fair served more as a playtest disguised as a presentation. I ended up learning a lot of things about how people reacted to the game that should have been discovered in advance and accounted.

My table by itself couldn’t really stand on its own. The game needed me to start it and the workshop didn’t have instructions inviting people to participate. Additionally, the learning curve for players was really steep and that made it hard for them to engage with the mechanics and really experiment with the floppy disks.

I’ve said this before, but this is the first project in which I was designing with purpose in mind. I struggled immensely with how to involve meaning and design for a target audience. And, during the fair, I wasn’t able to articulate that aspect of my project. A part of it was because I spent most of my time teaching audience members how to play the game, but that is a failure on my part for not developing a tutorial for the game. I had controls for my poster, but I forgot to account for joystick movement and I put my poster too far away from the play area.

Additionally, my table requires a lot of invested time if you want to experience everything. The VR experience is already lengthy but the glitching workshop also took quite some time. Glitching is unpredictable, so some people would take some time before any noticeable changes would appear on the image. However, I think this is inevitable for my project.

If I were to do it over again, I would have informational graphics inside the game to help teach the controls. I would also place a piece of paper that had information about using the glitch workshop.

## **Overall**

At the beginning of HDCC201, my professor Dr. Feldman had us write anxieties we had for our capstone. One of the things I wrote was that I was scared I wouldn’t grow from the process.   
Looking back at my work, I think that I have at least a little.  
I learned a lot more about the Unity game engine and acquired the fundamentals of 3D modeling with Blender. I have grown a lot in terms of technical skill.  
In terms of growing as a person, I managed to develop some techniques for combatting procrastination. Designing with purpose also made me rethink how I approached creating.

# **Moving Forward**

I plan to explore this concept of glitching more in the summer at the New Works Incubator program.  
I would really like to explore other possible modes for glitching like projection mapping.  
I am really grateful to have done this capstone project, and I am extremely thankful for Dr. Lu for her feedback and constant pushing for me to always think about purpose and how to appeal to people not interested. I am also thankful to my HDCC209 class for their inspiring projects and discussions.
